text: Ow, that stings. Wait, why does this only happen in winter?
Just your clothes brushing against your skin builds up a little static electricity on your body.
In summer, moisture in the air keeps draining that charge away. Winter air is just too dry for that.
So the moment you touch something like a metal doorknob, all that built-up charge rushes out at once - and that's the zap.

Actually, the word "electricity" comes from the Greek word for amber. Ancient Greeks noticed that rubbing amber made light things stick to it - that's the first time people ever noticed electricity at all.
The voltage in that spark is actually pretty high, often higher than your wall outlet. But the current is so tiny, it's not dangerous.
Some people say touching a metal key first, instead of your finger, makes the zap less painful.
